facts: $\mathrm{cbs}(f) = \mathrm{bs}(f)$ for Boolean $f$; the measure only says something new when an input has several valid answers.

Lifting: $\mathrm{R}^{cc}(S \circ g^n) = \Omega(\mathrm{cbs}(S))$ for a suitable constant-size gadget $g$ [GoosPitassi14]. This is the source of the tight monotone-circuit-depth and Cutting-Planes lower bounds obtained there.

For the false-clause search problem of a random $\Delta$-dense unsatisfiable $k$-CNF, $\mathrm{cbs} = \Omega(n)$; for the Tseitin search problem on a bounded-degree expander, $\mathrm{cbs} = \Omega(n)$ [GoosPitassi14].
The min over solution functions is essential: the maximum over $s$ can be large for trivially easy search problems.

The max over critical inputs is equally essential, and it cuts the other way: a search problem in which every input has at least two valid answers has no critical inputs at all, so the max is over the empty set and $\mathrm{cbs} = 0$. \(\mathrm{Find1}_{\ge n/2}\), \(\mathrm{ApproxHW}\) and \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\) are of this kind, and there $\mathrm{cbs}$ certifies nothing whatsoever -- not a weak bound but no bound, so the relational column reads $\infty$ against it.
self.name: Critical block sensitivity
self.short: Block sensitivity of a search problem: the adversary picks the input, but the algorithm picks which valid answer to commit to.

up.note: Let $s$ be the plurality output of a bounded-error algorithm $A$ of cost $T$, let $x$ be critical, and let $B_1,\dots,B_b$ be disjoint blocks with $s(x^{B_i}) \ne s(x)$. If $A$ never queries inside $B_i$ it behaves identically on $x$ and $x^{B_i}$, so it cannot output both answers with high probability; each block must therefore be entered with constant probability, giving $b = O(T)$. Taking the min over solution functions, $\mathrm{cbs} = O(\mathrm{R})$. The same conclusion follows from $\mathrm{cbs} = O(\mathrm{CA})$ [ABK21lifting] together with $\mathrm{CA} \le \mathrm{R}$.

up.note: The classical adversary dominates critical block sensitivity, for partial functions and search problems alike. This is what makes \(\mathrm{CA}(f)\) the stronger of the two as a lifting target: [ABK21lifting] lift $\mathrm{CAdv}$ to randomized communication complexity with a constant-size gadget, and the resulting lower bound is strictly stronger than the one lifting $\mathrm{cbs}$ gives. The converse fails to be tight -- see the $\mathrm{CA}$ vs $\mathrm{cbs}$ cell above, where $\vee_n$ shows the two can also coincide.

lo.note:
A single character has sparsity $1$ and $\mathrm{osss} = 1$: the two agree, but neither
grows, so this witnesses no exponent. No function in the zoo has $\mathrm{osss}$ growing
while $\mathrm{spar}$ stays bounded -- indeed $\mathrm{spar}(f) = O(1)$ forces $f$ to be a
constant-size combination of characters, and $\mathrm{osss}$ is then bounded too.
